state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain how changing all the plant heights by the same proportion might impact the range? Have you considered what the definition of range is and how changing the values could affect it?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so range is like the difference between the biggest and smallest number, right? So if all the plants are cut in half, both the biggest and smallest get smaller by half, so the difference between them would also get smaller... but I'm still confused about Katie's one because if you add 3 cm to everything, doesn't that change the range too?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's a great observation about how cutting the plants in half would affect the range. Now, let's think about how adding 3 cm to each plant might impact the range. Can you walk me through your thought process on how this change would affect the range based on the definition you mentioned earlier?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: So like, if I add 3 cm to the biggest plant and 3 cm to the smallest plant, they both go up by the same amount, so the difference between them stays the same, right? But that's different from cutting them in half because when you cut them in half, you're making the difference smaller... so does that mean Katie is actually right and Tom is wrong?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the proportional change misconception through well-calibrated questioning that leads the student to independently discover that Katie is right (additive changes preserve range) while Tom is wrong (multiplicative changes do not), demonstrating clear conceptual progress.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never directly provides the answer, and allows the student to discover through their own reasoning that their initial conclusion was incorrect.
